While the genre reached its peak of popularity during the 1930s with classics such as The Adventures of Robin Hood and The Sea Hawk, Disney's Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl essentially reimagined the swashbuckler for modern moviegoers while still tipping its hat to the classic tropes and treasures of the genre.

blocks.x: Kevin Reynolds' The Count of Monte Cristo is a marvelous adaptation of Alexandre Dumas' 1844 novel of the same name and is a superb pick for Pirates of the Caribbean fans who want a swashbuckler with a darker, more satisfying edge. The movie tells the story of Edmond Dantès (Jim Caviezel), a sailor wrongly imprisoned and left to rot in the island prison of Château d'If by his close friend (Guy Pearce), who escapes to claim a fortune and exact elaborate revenge against those who betrayed him.

Like the Pirates of the Caribbean films, The Count of Monte Cristo is full of seafaring adventure, from a daring prison break to encounters with smugglers and a thrilling final duel. The swordplay is crisp and dramatic, and the sweeping coastal landscapes and period costumes give it a lavish, old-fashioned feel, immersing audiences into an intense journey of redemption and vengeance. Caviezel brings charisma and intensity to Dantès, while Pearce is deliciously hateful as the smug, treacherous Fernand Mondego. Their rivalry drives the story, and the payoff is endlessly rewarding. Other notable performances include Richard Harris, as the wise Abbé Faria, and Luis Guzmán, as the scene-stealing smuggler Jacopo, who both add warmth and humor along the way.

blocks.c: Errol Flynn as Robin Hood in The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938)

blocks.x: There's no denying that The Adventures of Robin Hood defined the swashbuckler genre and any fan of Pirates of the Caribbean owes this classic at least one watch. Based on the English folklore legend, Errol Flynn stars as the Saxton knight turned outlaw with a heart of gold, Sir Robin of Locksley, who, along with his men and help from the lovely Maid Marian (Olivia de Havilland), fights to protect England and prevent the merciless Prince John (Claude Rains) from stealing the crown from his brother, Richard the Lionheart (Ian Hunter).

Flynn, without question, set the golden standard of the charming rogue with his impeccable performance, making him an icon of the swashbuckler genre. His Robin Hood laughs in the face of danger, taunts his enemies, and wins hearts with confidence and a mischievous grin. It's easy to see his influence on Captain Jack Sparrow, a hero who survives as much on wit and showmanship as on skill with a blade. The movie was one of the highest-grossing films of the year and went on to win three Oscars, notably for Best Original Score and Best Art Direction. While some might be put off by the age of the film, The Adventures of Robin Hood provided the blueprint for everything that makes swashbucklers so much fun, and is still a worthwhile watch for audiences today.

blocks.c: Collider logo
Westley with a wounded shoulder stands on guard with his sword while Buttercup stands behind him in The Princess Bride

blocks.x: Rob Reiner's swashbuckling adventure The Princess Bride is one of the greatest fantasy cult classics that wins you over with wit as much as swordplay, which is exactly why Pirates of the Caribbean fans should seek it out. Based on William Goldman's novel of the same name, the movie follows a swashbuckling farmhand, Wesley (Cary Elwes), who, after being away for five years and presumed dead, returns home where he sets out to rescue his true love, Buttercup (Robin Wright), from the evil Prince Humperdinck (Chris Sarandon).

While the story captivates audiences with fairy tale nostalgia and unpredictable humor, the swordplay in The Princess Bride is a main highlight, ultimately setting it apart from other modern swashbuckling adventures. The cliffside duel between Elwes and Mandy Patinkin's Inigo is a masterclass in banter and elegance, as two skilled fencers trade compliments and jabs, and the final showdown is just as satisfying. Add Wallace Shawn's scheming Vizzini, Andre the Giant's gentle Fezzik brings heart and humor, and a wonderfully theatrical Billy Crystal, and the villains and supporting players are unforgettable. Beneath the jokes and humorous antics lies a sincere love story and a loving tribute to classic adventure tales, proving that a great swashbuckler needs just as much heart as it does a sword.

bleeding, and extremely funny about it.

You share that stubbornness. Adversity doesn't make you noble, it makes you sarcastic,
and then it makes you unstoppable.

You'd thrive here because these films reward improvisation and nerve over preparation,
and you've never had the luxury of preparing anyway.

You didn't want any of this. You just declined to be the person who let it happen.

'The Count of Monte Cristo' (2002)

Kevin Reynolds' The Count of Monte Cristo is a marvelous adaptation of Alexandre Dumas' 1844 novel of the same name and is a superb pick for Pirates of the Caribbean fans who want a swashbuckler with a darker, more satisfying edge. The movie tells the story of Edmond Dantès (Jim Caviezel), a sailor wrongly imprisoned and left to rot in the island prison of Château d'If by his close friend (Guy Pearce), who escapes to claim a fortune and exact elaborate revenge against those who betrayed him.

Like the Pirates of the Caribbean films, The Count of Monte Cristo is full of seafaring adventure, from a daring prison break to encounters with smugglers and a thrilling final duel. The swordplay is crisp and dramatic, and the sweeping coastal landscapes and period costumes give it a lavish, old-fashioned feel, immersing audiences into an intense journey of redemption and vengeance. Caviezel brings charisma and intensity to Dantès, while Pearce is deliciously hateful as the smug, treacherous Fernand Mondego. Their rivalry drives the story, and the payoff is endlessly rewarding. Other notable performances include Richard Harris, as the wise Abbé Faria, and Luis Guzmán, as the scene-stealing smuggler Jacopo, who both add warmth and humor along the way.

2
'The Adventures of Robin Hood' (1938)

Image via Warner Bros. Pictures

There's no denying that The Adventures of Robin Hood defined the swashbuckler genre and any fan of Pirates of the Caribbean owes this classic at least one watch. Based on the English folklore legend, Errol Flynn stars as the Saxton knight turned outlaw with a heart of gold, Sir Robin of Locksley, who, along with his men and help from the lovely Maid Marian (Olivia de Havilland), fights to protect England and prevent the merciless Prince John (Claude Rains) from stealing the crown from his brother, Richard the Lionheart (Ian Hunter).

Flynn, without question, set the golden standard of the charming rogue with his impeccable performance, making him an icon of the swashbuckler genre. His Robin Hood laughs in the face of danger, taunts his enemies, and wins hearts with confidence and a mischievous grin. It's easy to see his influence on Captain Jack Sparrow, a hero who survives as much on wit and showmanship as on skill with a blade. The movie was one of the highest-grossing films of the year and went on to win three Oscars, notably for Best Original Score and Best Art Direction. While some might be put off by the age of the film, The Adventures of Robin Hood provided the blueprint for everything that makes swashbucklers so much fun, and is still a worthwhile watch for audiences today.

1
'The Princess Bride' (1987)

Image via 20th Century Studios

Rob Reiner's swashbuckling adventure The Princess Bride is one of the greatest fantasy cult classics that wins you over with wit as much as swordplay, which is exactly why Pirates of the Caribbean fans should seek it out. Based on William Goldman's novel of the same name, the movie follows a swashbuckling farmhand, Wesley (Cary Elwes), who, after being away for five years and presumed dead, returns home where he sets out to rescue his true love, Buttercup (Robin Wright), from the evil Prince Humperdinck (Chris Sarandon).

While the story captivates audiences with fairy tale nostalgia and unpredictable humor, the swordplay in The Princess Bride is a main highlight, ultimately setting it apart from other modern swashbuckling adventures. The cliffside duel between Elwes and Mandy Patinkin's Inigo is a masterclass in banter and elegance, as two skilled fencers trade compliments and jabs, and the final showdown is just as satisfying. Add Wallace Shawn's scheming Vizzini, Andre the Giant's gentle Fezzik brings heart and humor, and a wonderfully theatrical Billy Crystal, and the villains and supporting players are unforgettable. Beneath the jokes and humorous antics lies a sincere love story and a loving tribute to classic adventure tales, proving that a great swashbuckler needs just as much heart as it does a sword.
